claims.text: A combinatorial high-throughput thin-film approach can reveal how the relative percentages of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect mechanical properties.
Controlled co-alloying increments can reveal how the relative percentages of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect mechanical properties.
The initial material is a near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
The fractions of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr will be varied systematically using combinatorial deposition or multi-step co-alloying.
Post-processing heat treatment and ambient-temperature testing will provide a consistent and stable microstructure before mechanical measurements.
Changes in relative elemental concentrations produce changes in local chemical ordering.
Changes in relative elemental concentrations produce lattice distortions.
Changes in relative elemental concentrations produce changes in defect structures.
Element-dependent changes in solid-solution strengthening and lattice mismatch drive changes in mechanical behavior.
Incremental compositional changes will produce monotonic or intermediate shifts in mechanical properties.
Composition-dependent mechanical-property shifts can identify which elements dominate strengthening or ductility enhancement.
Large deviations from equiatomic ratios may cause nonlinear composition-property behavior.
Large deviations from equiatomic ratios may lead to phase transformations or secondary-phase formation.
Hardness and yield strength can be measured by nanoindentation and microcompression while phase and microstructure are characterized by XRD and electron microscopy.
